body.text: Reserve Bank's mission to reduce inflation may cost your neighbour their job
The Reserve Bank has acknowledged that more people are losing faith in its ability to control inflation in the next 12 months.

It says it is taking the matter seriously because "trust" plays an important role in the bank's ability to manage people's inflation expectations, which feed back into the bank's ability to control inflation.
RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser talked about it in a speech last week.
The ABC covered the speech here, with a focus on its main message.
But it is worth revisiting elements of the speech where Mr Hauser talked about the RBA's "values" and "full employment", for more interrogation.
Because they begged a question: do Australians know what the bank actually means when it talks about "full employment"?
And does the bank's modern usage of the term make people have more, or less, trust in its inflation-fighting approach and its ability to hit its inflation target?
When do we experience full employment?
Mr Hauser said the full impact of a rate hike depends on whether people "trust" the bank to do what is necessary to meet its inflation target.

By that he meant, if people believe the RBA will keep lifting rates until inflation comes down, that "belief" will influence their spending decisions, which will ultimately help the bank to control inflation.
"In simple terms, do they expect us to return the economy to balance, with on-target inflation and full employment, in the long run?" he asked.
But in the Q&A portion of his speech, Hauser was asked a fascinating question from the audience about the link between trust, accountability, and full employment:
"Trust needs something people can check you against," the audience member said.
"With inflation, that's the [RBA's] target band. [But] with full employment, there isn't an observable one.
"And when your estimate of [full employment] changes … that can look like [you're] moving the goalposts.
"So how can people hold you to account on that side of your mandate other than waiting to see what inflation does?"
It was a penetrating question, because what is full employment these days?
In email correspondence with the ABC, one of the complaints readers often have is about the modern meaning of the term.

Millions of older Australians remember when full employment was associated with an unemployment rate of roughly 2 per cent, when the labour market was overwhelmingly comprised of full-time jobs, when jobs were relatively abundant, and when loyalty to an employer was typically rewarded with predictable career progression and regular pay increases.
Today, full employment means something very different.

Today, it refers to the level of unemployment (and assorted other 'indicators') that coincides with a situation in which the total level of demand and supply in the economy is in "equilibrium", and where wage growth is steady enough that inflation is low and manageable and is not accelerating.
But depending on the state of the world, that could mean the economy is in full employment when the unemployment rate is around 5 per cent, or 6 per cent, or 7 per cent, or higher.
That is not what full employment used to mean.
What's in a word?
Mr Hauser was delivering the annual Sir Leslie Melville Lecture. Melville (1902-2002) was a titan of Australian economics in the 20th century.

Hauser reminded his audience that Melville helped to shape the intellectual foundations for clause 8 of the Commonwealth Bank Act 1945, which set the bank's dual mandate of price stability (originally, stability of the currency) and "the maintenance of full employment."
"That mission remains fundamentally unchanged. It shapes everything we do," Hauser said in his speech.
But is that literally true, what Hauser said?
The meaning of "full employment" today is fundamentally different from its original meaning.

The phrase is a relic from the post-World War II era when Australia's economic, institutional, and cultural context was thoroughly different. It comes from a time when politicians were ashamed if unemployment increased.
Australia's policymakers waved goodbye to "full employment" in the mid-1970s.
They then cycled through various models of economic management before stumbling upon inflation-targeting in the early 1990s.

And when they adopted inflation-targeting, they had to develop an updated definition of "full employment" to fit their new method of economic management, which would allow the bank to keep meeting its full employment mandate.
So, the words "full employment" have remained in the RBA's mandate, but their insides have changed; it is like removing a kilogram of gold from your backpack and replacing it with a kilogram of sand.
Measuring modern full employment
The point the audience member (at Hauser's speech) was making about the link between trust, accountability and full employment was therefore insightful.
Since full employment is not observable anymore, how do people know if the RBA is delivering that part of its mandate?
Hauser said the RBA tries to draw together a range of measures of what it "feels like" when you're at full employment to give a sense of how close we may be to it.
See the graphic below
At the moment, according to those measures, the RBA says a majority of labour market indicators still appear close to, or slightly tighter than, their estimated trend levels.
That means the RBA thinks employment is still a bit too "full" at the moment and it needs to get less full to slow inflation down.
The unemployment rate is currently 4.7 per cent, but the bank is forecasting the unemployment rate will need to rise to 5.1 per cent by December 2028 to secure the necessary disinflation.
Unemployment for thee, less inflation for me?

Now, on the question of whether there is an alternative to managing inflation, instead of using the unemployed and mortgage-holders as shock absorbers, that debate is getting livelier as each year passes.
But in his Q&A, Hauser made an observation relevant to that debate.

He said the RBA made the decision in 2022 and 2023 to raise rates by a little less than some other countries, knowing it would mean that inflation would take a little longer to come down in Australia, to preserve as many of the gains in employment as possible that Australia made in the aftermath of COVID.
But looking back, given the anger people feel about inflation now, was that the right decision?
"Inflation is experienced by everyone, and unemployment, sadly, is only experienced by those who are unemployed or … in some cases, indirectly attached to it," Hauser said.
"So that has been a very live issue.

"We have tried to explain that, but obviously one person's benefit — 'Thanks very much, I'm still in a job' — may be another person's, 'Wow, you've let inflation remain pretty high for a long period of time,'" he said.
Hauser was making an uncomfortable point about human psychology.
High inflation hits you and your neighbour (not equally, mind you), but if you could lower inflation for everyone by pushing your neighbour into unemployment, would you do it?

Some people who seem like they would relish that choice have been giving the RBA a lot of free advice in recent years about the need to crank interest rates higher and faster than the bank has felt comfortable doing.
